analysis.explanation: The Random Forest predicts MALWARE at 0.9950, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with a combined SHAP contribution of about +0.169. No n-gram pushes the other way. The n-grams fall into three groups that match the compute profile of mining and hashing code. (1) Rotate/add chains: MOV ROL (+0.010191), ROL ADD (+0.009027), ADD ROL (+0.007947), ADD ROR (+0.007418), ROL MOV (+0.006077) and CMP ROL (+0.005880) resemble the add-rotate-xor rounds of hash and cipher primitives. (2) SIMD state handling: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.022089, the strongest feature), PXOR MOVUPS (+0.014970), MOVUPS PXOR (+0.006138), PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.005636) and ADD MOVQ (+0.005606) suggest vectorized XOR/add mixing of wide state blocks. (3) Floating-point and bit-scan operations: ADD CVTSI2SD (+0.007062) and CVTSI2SD MULSD (+0.006321) indicate integer-to-double conversion and multiplication, while BSF MOV (+0.006178) and DEC BSR (+0.005726) indicate bit-scan arithmetic. Together these suggest a mixed integer, vector and floating-point workload. Several of these patterns also occur in legitimate crypto, compression or math libraries, and the evidence lists no functions or call context. The frequencies are also all very small (at most 0.000413). The conclusion therefore rests on the breadth and consistency of the signals plus the very high model probability, not on any single n-gram. I assign high confidence, with the caveat that it is inferred from instruction patterns only.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Strongest contributor. Aligned SIMD XOR followed by a 128-bit move is typical of vectorized state mixing or scratchpad handling in hashing and mining loops.
Unaligned SIMD XOR and store. It reinforces the vectorized XOR-mixing pattern and is consistent with bulk state manipulation in hash kernels.
A call directly followed by a return suggests thunks, tail-call stubs or small wrappers. Alone it is weak, but the model treats it as a strong malware-associated structural pattern.
Loading a value and then rotating it is a hallmark of ARX-style hash and cipher rounds.
Rotate then add is a core ARX step found in hash functions used in proof-of-work.
A common sign-test branch. It is the most frequent n-gram here (0.000413), so it is likely generic loop or conditional control flow, with modest independent diagnostic value.
An unusual control-flow idiom that can indicate indirect jumps or obfuscated transfers. The model treats it as a malware-associated trait.
Add followed by rotate, the reverse order of ROL ADD. Together they indicate repeated ARX round structure.
Branchless conditional selection after a subtraction, often used in constant-time or tight numeric loops. It is consistent with optimized compute code.
Add followed by rotate-right, another ARX-style hashing primitive that complements the ROL-based patterns.
Integer arithmetic feeding a conversion to double precision. It suggests a mixed integer/floating-point pipeline, as in some memory-hard or randomized-execution mining algorithms.
Integer-to-double conversion followed by a floating-point multiply. This supports a floating-point compute component, though it is also common in ordinary numeric code.
Bit-scan-forward use indicates low-level bit manipulation, common in optimized hashing and big-integer routines, but also in string and memory utilities.
Load of a 128-bit value followed by XOR, the mirror of PXOR MOVUPS. Together they indicate a load-XOR-store mixing cycle.
A rotate whose result is moved onward fits the rotate-heavy dataflow of hash round functions.
A compare adjacent to a rotate suggests round-counter loop control around rotate-based computation.
Decrement and bit-scan-reverse suggest bit-length or leading-zero computations, as in big-number arithmetic or difficulty/target comparisons. This is speculative from the n-gram alone.

A SIMD byte-compare and mask-extract idiom, typical of vectorized string or memory scanning (e.g. strlen/memchr). It is likely generic runtime code, but the model still counts it toward the malware prediction.
64-bit packed addition followed by an aligned move. It fits vectorized arithmetic on wide state, in line with the other SIMD features.
Integer add feeding a 64-bit SIMD/GPR move shows interplay between scalar and vector registers, as in optimized crypto kernels.

key_indicators: Random Forest malware probability of 0.9950 with all 20 top SHAP contributions positive (sum about +0.169)
Dense rotate/add n-gram family (MOV ROL, ROL ADD, ADD ROL, ADD ROR, ROL MOV, CMP ROL) consistent with ARX hash rounds
Top-ranked SIMD XOR/move patterns (PXOR MOVAPS +0.022089, PXOR MOVUPS +0.014970, MOVUPS PXOR) indicating vectorized state mixing
Floating-point conversion and multiply (ADD CVTSI2SD, CVTSI2SD MULSD) alongside integer and vector operations
Bit-scan and branchless-select idioms (BSF MOV, DEC BSR, SUB CMOVG) typical of optimized numeric kernels
Unusual control-flow idioms (CALL RET, PUSH RET) weighted toward malware
analysis.recommended_action: Treat the sample as a likely cryptojacker and quarantine it. Confirm with dynamic or sandbox analysis: look for sustained high CPU use, mining-pool or stratum network traffic, and wallet or pool strings and configuration. In static analysis, locate the code regions containing the rotate/add and PXOR/MOVAPS/MOVUPS sequences and check whether they implement a known hash or mining algorithm. The evidence lists no functions or call context and the n-gram frequencies are very low, so this pattern-based verdict should be corroborated before final attribution.
